title: Tested in the Wilderness, Rejected at Home
summary: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is tested by the devil for forty days in the wilderness and answers each temptation from Deuteronomy. Back in Galilee he reads Isaiah 61 in the Nazareth synagogue and announces that it is fulfilled today, but his hometown turns on him when he recalls God's mercy to foreigners. In Capernaum he drives out an unclean spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and many others, and then moves on to preach the kingdom of God in other towns.
story:
At the Jordan the Father named Jesus his beloved Son, and the genealogy traced him back to Adam, the son of God. Now that sonship is tested. Where Adam fell in a garden and Israel grumbled through forty years in the wilderness, Jesus holds firm in the wilderness for forty days, and he does it with the words Moses spoke to Israel about its own testing. The devil withdraws, but only until an opportune time, and Luke will bring him back when Judas betrays Jesus (22:3).

Then Luke opens the public ministry with a scene he places first on purpose: the sermon in Nazareth. Mark and Matthew tell of a visit to Nazareth later in the story; Luke moves it to the front and makes it a program for everything that follows. Good news for the poor, release for captives, sight for the blind, a mercy that reaches beyond Israel, and rejection by his own people are all here in miniature, and the attempt to throw Jesus from a cliff outside his town casts the shadow of the cross over the first day of his preaching. The rest of the chapter shows the announcement becoming deed in Capernaum, a single Sabbath day and evening in which Jesus teaches with authority, frees a man from an unclean spirit, heals a fever, and lays hands on the sick one by one. When the town tries to keep him, he refuses: the kingdom must be announced elsewhere too, because that is why he was sent.
historical:
Galilee, the northern region where Jesus grew up and did most of his work, was ruled from 4 BC to AD 39 by Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, as tetrarch under Rome (Josephus, Antiquities 17.318, 18.252). It was largely Jewish in the first century, a land of farming villages in the hills and fishing towns around the lake. Antipas rebuilt Sepphoris, about four miles north of Nazareth, as the ornament of all Galilee (Antiquities 18.27), and later founded Tiberias on the lakeshore around AD 19 or 20 and made it his capital (Antiquities 18.36-38). Neither city is mentioned in the Gospels.

Nazareth itself was a small hill village. It appears nowhere in the Old Testament, Josephus, or the Mishnah, and the earliest non-Christian mention is a Hebrew inscription of the priestly courses from Caesarea, of the third or fourth century. Excavations show a modest farming settlement. In 2009 Yardenna Alexandre of the Israel Antiquities Authority published a house of the early Roman period near the Church of the Annunciation, with pottery and stone vessels of the kind Jewish families used for ritual purity, and estimated the village at roughly fifty houses on a few acres. No first-century synagogue building has been found there, which is no surprise, since in a village the gathering could meet in a large house or courtyard.

Capernaum sat on the northwest shore of the lake, near the border with the territory of Antipas's half-brother Philip, which made it a natural place for a toll station (5:27). Jonathan Reed (Archaeology and the Galilean Jesus, 2000) estimated its population at around a thousand. The white limestone synagogue that visitors see today was dated by its excavators, the Franciscans Virgilio Corbo and Stanislao Loffreda, to the late fourth or fifth century on the evidence of thousands of coins and pottery sealed beneath its floors; others have argued for the third century. Beneath it lie walls and a floor of the local black basalt that Loffreda assigned to the first century and identified with the synagogue of Jesus' day, a public building on the same plot. The identification is reasonable though not certain. Nearby, beneath a fifth-century octagonal church, excavators found a first-century house whose main room was later plastered and set apart for gatherings, its walls eventually scratched with Christian graffiti. The pilgrim Egeria, around 381 to 384, described a house at Capernaum turned into a church with its original walls still standing, identified as Peter's (the passage survives through Peter the Deacon's twelfth-century compilation).

The temptation's third scene takes place on the pterugion of the temple, some high edge of Herod's vast rebuilding, which began around 20 BC and was still under way in Jesus' lifetime. Josephus says that anyone looking down from the roof of the Royal Portico on the south side into the Kidron valley grew dizzy (Antiquities 15.411-412). Mark 6:1-6 and Matthew 13:53-58 also tell of Jesus' rejection at Nazareth but place it later and give no synagogue reading; Luke's reference in verse 23 to what Jesus had already done in Capernaum shows he knows the visit did not come first in time.
cultural:
A synagogue (from a Greek word for a gathering) was a local assembly and its meeting place for prayer, the reading of Scripture, and teaching. The Theodotus inscription from Jerusalem, dated by most scholars before AD 70, says the building it commemorates was made for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments. Josephus (Against Apion 2.175) and Philo describe weekly gatherings to hear and learn the Law, and Acts 13:15 describes a service at Pisidian Antioch with a reading from the Law and the Prophets followed by an invitation to speak. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200, describes a reading from the Law followed by one from the Prophets (the haftarah) and allows the reader of the Prophets to skip from place to place (m. Megillah 4:4). Whether the prophetic reading was already fixed in a cycle in Jesus' day is unknown; the details of Luke's scene (he found the place) may mean Jesus chose it. Readers stood out of respect for the text and teachers sat, and the attendant (ḥazzan) took the scroll back. Scrolls were long: the great Isaiah scroll from Qumran (1QIsaiah-a) is over seven meters, with chapter 61 near the end.

The words Jesus reads come from Isaiah 61:1-2, with the line ‘to release the oppressed’ drawn from Isaiah 58:6 and Isaiah's ‘to bind up the brokenhearted’ left out in the best manuscripts. Isaiah's liberty (deror) and ‘year of favor’ echo the Jubilee of Leviticus 25, the fiftieth year announced by the ram's horn on the Day of Atonement (25:9), when Israelite slaves went free and family land returned to its clans. There is no clear record that the Jubilee was ever carried out in full, and Jeremiah 34 tells of a release of slaves that was quickly reversed, but the hope behind it grew. At Qumran the Melchizedek text (11Q13) weaves Leviticus 25, Deuteronomy 15, and Isaiah 61 into a vision of a final Jubilee of release and atonement, and 4Q521 expects God to heal the wounded, raise the dead, and bring good news to the poor. Isaiah 58, the source of the inserted line, is still the haftarah read in synagogues on the morning of Yom Kippur (Isaiah 57:14-58:14), a fitting partner for a Jubilee announced on the Day of Atonement.

Jesus stops mid-sentence, before Isaiah's next words, “and the day of our God’s vengeance” (Isaiah 61:2). His examples of Elijah and Elisha would have stung. In 1 Kings 17 God sent Elijah in a famine to a widow in Zarephath, a Phoenician town in the heartland of the Baal worship of Jezebel's father, and in 2 Kings 5 Elisha cleansed Naaman, commander of the army of Aram, Israel's enemy. The proverb ‘Physician, heal yourself’ was widespread; Genesis Rabbah 23:4 preserves a Hebrew form about a physician healing his own limp. Demons and unclean spirits were a vivid part of the world of Luke's readers: Tobit 6-8 tells of driving out a demon with smoke from a fish's heart and liver, and Josephus describes a Jewish exorcist, Eleazar, drawing out a demon through a man's nose with a ring and a root prescribed by Solomon before Vespasian (Antiquities 8.46-48). Against that background Jesus uses no ring, root, or incantation, only a command. At sunset (verse 40) the Sabbath ended and carrying the sick was again permitted (compare Jeremiah 17:21-22 and m. Shabbat 7:2, where carrying from one domain to another is among the forbidden kinds of work).
literary:
The temptation has three rounds, each built the same way: the devil's offer and Jesus' answer from Deuteronomy (8:3, 6:13, 6:16), the book in which Moses reminds Israel of its own testing in the wilderness. The parallel is exact and intended. Israel was God's son (Exodus 4:22), was led forty years in the wilderness to be humbled and tested (Deuteronomy 8:2), hungered and grumbled for bread, was warned against worshiping other gods, and tested the LORD at Massah. Jesus, the Son, is led by the Spirit for forty days, hungers, and at each point answers as Israel should have. In the third round the devil quotes Scripture too (Psalm 91:11-12), leaving out ‘in all your ways’, so that the Bible itself becomes the tempter's instrument. Matthew 4:1-11 has the same three tests but orders them bread, temple, mountain, ending with the offer of the kingdoms and Jesus' command to Satan to go. Luke orders them bread, kingdoms, temple, ending in Jerusalem at the temple, the city where his Gospel begins and ends and toward which his story moves from 9:51. Most scholars, Joseph Fitzmyer among them, think Matthew preserves the earlier order and Luke moved the temple scene last; the question remains open. Mark 1:12-13 tells the temptation in two verses without the dialogue.

The Nazareth scene is narrated with slow ceremony, and many interpreters have noticed that the actions around the reading form a mirror pattern: he stood up, was handed the scroll, unrolled it, found the place, read, rolled it up, returned it, sat down. At the center stands the reading, and after it the single sentence “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.” The mood then swings from admiration to fury in a few verses, turning on two sayings (the physician proverb and the unwelcome prophet) and two precedents (Elijah and Elisha), a pairing of a woman and a man that Luke likes (compare 2:25-38, 15:4-10). The word dektos, ‘acceptable’, links the ‘acceptable year of the Lord’ (verse 19) with the prophet who is not ‘acceptable’ at home (verse 24). The Capernaum episodes (31-44) follow Mark 1:21-39 closely but frame the day as the fulfillment of verse 18: the word with authority, release for the oppressed, and healing. Luke uses the verb ‘rebuke’ for the demon, the fever, and the demons at sunset alike, treating illness and evil as powers Jesus commands. The chapter closes with a summary and Jesus' first use of the phrase ‘the kingdom of God’ (verse 43), repeating the verb of Isaiah 61, ‘to preach good news’, and the verb ‘sent’, so that the end of the chapter answers its programmatic reading.

outline.t: Jesus returns to Galilee in the power of the Spirit
The reading from Isaiah in Nazareth
Elijah, Elisha, and the hometown's rejection
Authority over an unclean spirit in Capernaum
Sent to preach the kingdom in other towns

doctrines.note: Luke stresses the Spirit at every turn: Jesus is full of the Spirit, led by the Spirit in the wilderness, returns in the power of the Spirit, and reads that the Spirit of the Lord is on him because God has anointed him. His ministry is the Spirit's work, and the same Spirit will fill the church in Acts, where Peter describes how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power (Acts 10:38).

To be anointed is what the title Messiah (Hebrew) or Christ (Greek) means. Jesus claims Isaiah's Spirit-anointed herald as himself, the unclean spirit calls him the Holy One of God, and the demons at sunset know him as the Christ (verse 41). He is the Son of God whose sonship the devil tests and cannot bend.

The second temptation asks for worship in exchange for the kingdoms of the world, and Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:13: God alone is to be worshiped and served. The Son refuses to gain by bowing to evil the kingdom he will receive from the Father through obedience and the cross.

The first word of Jesus' public mission in Luke is good news to the poor, and the reading adds release for captives and the oppressed, drawing on Isaiah 58, where God rejects worship without justice for the hungry and the bound. Luke's Gospel will fill these words with people: a poor widow, lepers, the blind beggar, Zacchaeus's restitution.

The Nazareth sermon points outward: God's prophets were sent to a widow of Sidon and a Syrian general, and at the end of the chapter Jesus refuses to be kept by one town because he was sent to preach the kingdom to others. The pattern anticipates Acts, where the message moves from Jerusalem to the nations.

words.note: Peirazō, to test or tempt. It occurs about thirty-eight times in the New Testament and covers both a trial meant to prove someone and an enticement to do wrong; BDAG treats the two as distinct senses of one verb, and context decides. The same forty days are God's proving of his Son and the devil's attempt to make him fall. Its compound ekpeirazō, ‘put to the test’, used in verse 12 (from Deuteronomy 6:16), occurs only four times (Matthew 4:7, Luke 4:12, 10:25, 1 Corinthians 10:9), and the noun peirasmos closes the scene in verse 13.

Chriō, to anoint. It occurs only five times in the New Testament (Luke 4:18, Acts 4:27, 10:38, 2 Corinthians 1:21, Hebrews 1:9), and in all but the Corinthians passage God anoints Jesus. In the Old Testament kings, priests, and occasionally prophets (1 Kings 19:16) were anointed with oil to mark them for God's service, and from this verb comes christos, anointed one. Jesus is anointed not with oil but with the Spirit, which descended on him at the Jordan (3:22).

Euangelizomai, to announce good news. It occurs about fifty-four times in the New Testament, ten in Luke and fifteen in Acts, once in Matthew, and never in Mark or John, so it is characteristically Lukan. The Septuagint uses it for the herald of Isaiah 40:9, 52:7, and 61:1 who announces God's return and reign. Luke uses it in verse 18 from Isaiah and again in verse 43 of Jesus' own mission to preach the kingdom, making the herald of Isaiah the pattern for all Jesus' preaching.

Aphesis, release or forgiveness. It occurs seventeen times in the New Testament, ten of them in Luke and Acts, and appears twice in verse 18, for liberty to captives and release for the oppressed. In the Septuagint it names the Jubilee itself, the ‘year of release’ (Leviticus 25:10-13), and the cancellation of debts (Deuteronomy 15). Everywhere else in Luke and Acts it means the forgiveness of sins (1:77, 3:3, 24:47). Luke lets the two senses sit together without collapsing either into the other.

Dektos, acceptable, welcome, favorable. It occurs five times in the New Testament (Luke 4:19, 4:24, Acts 10:35, 2 Corinthians 6:2, Philippians 4:18). In the Septuagint it translates Hebrew ratson, ‘favor’, in Isaiah's ‘year of favor’ (61:2). Luke uses it twice in six verses: the year of the Lord's favor is announced, yet the prophet himself is not dektos, not welcome, in his hometown. Paul quotes the related verse Isaiah 49:8 when he says that now is the favorable time (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Sēmeron, today. It occurs about forty times in the New Testament, twenty of them in Luke and Acts. In Luke it marks the moments when God's long promises arrive in the present tense: today a Savior is born (2:11), today this Scripture is fulfilled (4:21), today salvation has come to this house (19:9), today you will be with me in Paradise (23:43). The word refuses to push fulfillment into an indefinite future.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. It occurs about a hundred times in the New Testament and sixteen times in Luke. In this chapter the devil offers Jesus authority over the kingdoms of the world (verse 6), claiming it has been handed over to him, and a few scenes later the people of Capernaum marvel that Jesus' word has authority (verse 32) and commands unclean spirits with authority and power (verse 36). The authority Jesus refused to take from the devil he already exercises from God.

christ:
Every temptation aims at the title just given at the baptism, “If You are the Son of God”, and invites Jesus to prove it on the devil's terms: to use his power for himself, to take the world's kingdoms without the cross, or to force God's hand with a spectacle. He refuses each time, choosing trust and obedience as the true Israel and the true son of Adam. Where Israel hungered and grumbled, he hungers and waits on his Father's word; where Israel turned to idols, he worships God alone; where Israel tested the LORD at Massah, he refuses to test him. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.21) saw here the second Adam undoing the first: the enemy who defeated a well-fed man through food could not persuade a hungry one, and the victory over the tempter is won by a man for all who descend from Adam. Hebrews draws the pastoral conclusion: “we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

At Nazareth Jesus claims to be the one Isaiah spoke of. In Isaiah 61 the speaker is an anointed herald of the return from exile; later Jewish readers linked the passage with a coming deliverer (11Q13 gives its language to a heavenly Melchizedek). Jesus says it is fulfilled today in their hearing. The fulfillment is not a program he will begin one day; it happens as he speaks, and Luke's later chapters show it happening: the poor hear good news (6:20, 7:22), captives of disease and Satan are released (13:16), the blind see (18:35-43), and sins are forgiven (5:20, 7:48). When John the Baptist later asks whether Jesus is the one to come, Jesus answers in the words of this reading (7:22).

The mercy to the widow of Zarephath and to Naaman points to the Gentile mission of Acts, and the rejection that follows, ending at the brow of a hill outside the town, foreshadows the cross, where he is led out of the city and mocked in the physician's proverb, he saved others; let him save himself (23:35). His walking away through the crowd shows that his life will be taken only when his hour comes (22:53). In Capernaum the unclean spirit calls him “the Holy One of God”, and his authority over evil, sickness, and the Sabbath's burdens shows the kingdom he announces already at work in his person.
interpretation:
The temptation has been read from the second century as the second Adam's victory. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.21, around 180) made it part of his teaching of recapitulation, Christ summing up and reversing Adam's story. Origen's homilies on Luke, preached at Caesarea and preserved in Jerome's Latin, treat both the temptation and the Nazareth reading, which Origen took as the Savior's announcement of release from sin. Gregory the Great, preaching on the first Sunday of Lent in 591 (Homilies on the Gospels 16), matched the three temptations to the three by which the serpent overcame Adam, through appetite, vainglory, and avarice, and taught that the devil overcame the first man and was overcome by the second by the same means. Many later writers linked the three to the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16). Thomas Aquinas discussed why Christ willed to be tempted (Summa Theologiae III, question 41).

Marcion of Sinope, around 144, began his Gospel with Jesus coming down to Capernaum in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, joining 3:1 to 4:31 and cutting out the birth, the baptism, the genealogy, the temptation, and the Nazareth reading of Israel's prophet; Tertullian answered him in Against Marcion 4.7. Among the Reformers, Luther and Calvin read the temptation as a pattern for the believer armed with the word of God, and commentators of every tradition have noticed that the devil's use of Psalm 91, without ‘in all your ways’, shows how Scripture torn from its context becomes a weapon against faith. John Milton's Paradise Regained (1671) is a four-book poem on the temptation that follows Luke's order, ending with the Son standing on the pinnacle as Satan falls. Fyodor Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor, in The Brothers Karamazov (1880), reads the three temptations as miracle, mystery, and authority, the means by which a church might rule people by offering bread and certainty rather than freedom.

The Nazareth sermon became central in modern interpretation, where commentators routinely call it programmatic for Luke-Acts. Robert Sloan (The Favorable Year of the Lord, 1977) and Sharon Ringe (Jesus, Liberation, and the Biblical Jubilee, 1985) traced its Jubilee theology; John Howard Yoder (The Politics of Jesus, 1972) argued that Jesus proclaimed a real Jubilee with social and economic demands, while others read the year of favor as the messianic age of salvation of which economic release is a sign. Latin American liberation theologians, following Gustavo Gutiérrez (A Theology of Liberation, 1971), made the passage a charter of God's preferential option for the poor, and the Jubilee 2000 campaign for cancelling the debts of poor nations drew on Leviticus 25 and this reading. Joachim Jeremias (Jesus' Promise to the Nations, 1958) argued that the hearers were offended by the omission of vengeance on the nations. Jewish scholars and Christian scholars in dialogue have asked how the scene has been used: Jack T. Sanders (The Jews in Luke-Acts, 1987) read Luke as hostile to the Jews, Jacob Jervell (Luke and the People of God, 1972) as a book about Israel divided and restored, and Amy-Jill Levine has warned preachers against making Jesus' hometown a symbol of Jewish narrowness.

In the church's worship, Luke 4:1-13 is the Gospel for the first Sunday in Lent in Year C of the Revised Common Lectionary, and the Lenten fast of forty days has always been tied to this story. Luke 4:14-21 and 4:21-30 are read on the third and fourth Sundays after the Epiphany in Year C. In art, Duccio's Temptation of Christ on the Mountain (from the Maestà, 1308 to 1311, now in the Frick Collection) shows the kingdoms as small walled cities at Jesus' feet, and Botticelli's fresco in the Sistine Chapel (1481 to 1482) sets the three temptations in the background of a temple scene.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles come from the manuscripts. In verse 4 the earliest manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, end the quotation at ‘bread alone’; Codex Alexandrinus and the later Byzantine text add ‘but by every word of God’, filled out from Matthew 4:4, which is why the King James Version is longer. In verse 5 the Byzantine text adds ‘the devil’ and ‘into a high mountain’ from Matthew 4:8, and in verse 8 it adds ‘Get behind me, Satan’, which the earliest witnesses lack. In verse 1 the best text reads that the Spirit led Jesus ‘in the wilderness’ (throughout the forty days), where later manuscripts read ‘into the wilderness’.

In verse 18 the Byzantine text and the King James Version include ‘to heal the brokenhearted’, a line from Isaiah 61:1 that is absent from Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and other early witnesses and was probably restored by scribes who knew Isaiah; modern editions omit it. In verse 17 Sinaiticus and most manuscripts say Jesus ‘unrolled’ the scroll, while Vaticanus and some others say he ‘opened’ it, a word better suited to a bound book; the sense is the same. In verse 44 the earliest witnesses (Papyrus 75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) say Jesus preached in the synagogues ‘of Judea’, while Alexandrinus, Bezae, and the Byzantine text read ‘of Galilee’, matching Mark 1:39. Editors prefer ‘Judea’ as the harder reading, understood in Luke's wide sense of the whole Jewish homeland (1:5, 23:5), and the King James Version's ‘Galilee’ reflects the correction.

Luke's quotation of Isaiah follows the Septuagint, not the Hebrew. Where the Hebrew speaks of ‘opening’ for prisoners, the Greek reads ‘recovery of sight to the blind’, which English Bibles translating Luke keep while their Isaiah 61:1 reads ‘freedom to the prisoners’. The inserted line ‘to release the oppressed’ comes from the Septuagint of Isaiah 58:6.

teach.big: Jesus, the Spirit-anointed Son who conquered temptation by trusting his Father's word, announces that God's year of release has arrived in him, a grace that reaches the poor and the outsider and that his own people find hard to receive.

outline.t: The Son is tested where Adam and Israel failed and wins by trusting and obeying God's word, not by using his power for himself; the devil's use of Scripture warns every reader.
The Spirit who led Jesus through testing now empowers his ministry, and early popularity is not the same as faith.
Jesus reads Isaiah and claims its promise as fulfilled today in himself: good news for the poor, release, sight, and the year of the Lord's favor, with the day of vengeance held back.
Familiarity and entitlement blind the hometown, and the reminder that God showed mercy to a Sidonian widow and a Syrian general turns admiration to violence.
In Capernaum Jesus' word carries authority that frees a man from an unclean spirit, without ritual or technique.
The same authority reaches a private sickbed and a town's sick at sunset, one by one, and the healed woman's first act is to serve.
Jesus refuses to be kept by one grateful town, because he was sent to preach the kingdom to others too.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first turns the temptation into a technique, as if quoting the right verse were a charm against temptation. Jesus answers with Scripture, but the answers express trust and obedience, and the devil can quote Scripture too; the point is the Son's faithful heart, not verse-matching. The second makes the story merely a moral example and misses its place in Israel's story: Jesus is the faithful Son where Israel failed, and his victory is first something done for us before it is a pattern for us. A third claims too much about the devil's offer in verse 6, as if Satan truly owned the world; Luke reports the claim without endorsing it, and the chapter shows Jesus holding real authority.

With the Nazareth scene, avoid two opposite reductions. One spiritualizes the poor, captives, and blind so completely that the words lose their plain sense; Luke's Gospel is full of literal poor people, prisoners of disease, and blind beggars. The other reduces the passage to a political program and loses the forgiveness of sins that aphesis carries through the rest of Luke and Acts. Avoid also presenting the people of Nazareth as typical of Jews in contrast to a universalist Jesus. The objections come from his own neighbors, and the precedents he cites come from Israel's own Scriptures and prophets; the warning is to every insider, including the church.
teach.pastoral: The temptation speaks to anyone who feels ashamed of being tempted. Being tested is not sin, and Jesus himself was tempted when he was hungry, alone, and weak; teachers can say so plainly to people who fear that their struggles mean they are beyond God's help. Be careful with the Nazareth scene where it touches on rejection by family or home church: Jesus was rejected by those who knew him longest, and people who have been pushed out of a family or congregation may find in him someone who understands. Avoid using the healing scenes to imply that the sick who are not healed lack faith; in this chapter the sick are brought by others, and Jesus lays his hands on each one.

hard.q: If Jesus was the Son of God and could not sin, was the temptation real?
hard.a:
The objection is sharp from two directions. From within the church, Charles Hodge (Systematic Theology, 1872 to 1873) argued that temptation implies the possibility of sinning: if it was impossible from the constitution of Christ's person for him to sin, his temptation was unreal and he could not truly sympathize with his people. From outside it, critics have doubted that the story is history at all. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) read it as a myth built from the testings of Israel, Moses, and Elijah, and Rudolf Bultmann (The History of the Synoptic Tradition, 1921) treated it as a secondary legend shaped in early Christian argument over Scripture. The skeptic adds a simple question: who was there to report it?

Christian responses divide on the first question and agree on more than they differ. Many classical theologians hold that Christ was impeccable, unable to sin, because his person is the eternal Son; W. G. T. Shedd (Dogmatic Theology, 1888) defended this against Hodge, arguing that a temptation can be real, felt and resisted to the end, even when its outcome is certain, and that the one who never yields feels temptation's full force as those who give in early never do. Others, with Hodge, hold that Christ in his human nature was able not to sin rather than unable to sin. Both positions confess that he was “without sin” (Hebrews 4:15), and neither is required by the creeds; the question is a second-order one about how to describe the union of two natures. On the historical question, defenders note that the story has the form of a report Jesus himself would have had to tell his disciples, since no one else was present, and that it is told in a thoroughly Jewish way, as a replay of Deuteronomy 6 to 8. Scholars such as Birger Gerhardsson (The Testing of God's Son, 1966) studied it as early Christian midrash on Deuteronomy, a genre judgment that does not settle whether it rests on an experience of Jesus. Luke's own interest is theological: the Son whose identity the Father declared is tested and proves faithful.

hard.q: Does the Nazareth scene, with its turn to the Gentiles and a mob of Jews trying to kill Jesus, set Luke against the Jewish people?
hard.a:
The objection deserves its strongest form. Jack T. Sanders (The Jews in Luke-Acts, 1987) argued that Luke-Acts is fundamentally hostile to the Jews: the Nazareth story announces at the outset a pattern in which Jews reject God's messengers and the gospel passes to the Gentiles, repeated in Acts until Paul's final words in Rome (Acts 28:25-28). Jewish readers have felt the weight of this pattern in centuries of Christian preaching that made Jews the people who reject and kill prophets. Amy-Jill Levine and others have warned that sermons on this passage often contrast a generous, universal Jesus with a narrow, nationalist Judaism, a contrast that misrepresents first-century Judaism and has fed contempt.

Other readers answer from the text. Jacob Jervell (Luke and the People of God, 1972) argued that Luke describes not Israel's rejection but its division: many thousands of Jews believe (Acts 2:41, 21:20), and the church is restored Israel into which Gentiles are welcomed. Jesus' precedents come from Israel's own Scriptures, and his claim is that of a Jewish prophet speaking to his own people, as Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, and Amos did. The hearers in Nazareth are neighbors offended by a familiar man's claim and by the thought that God's favor might pass them by, a temptation Luke's Christian readers share. Robert Tannehill (The Narrative Unity of Luke-Acts, 1986 and 1990) read the rejection of Jesus by Israel as a tragedy Luke grieves, not a triumph he celebrates. The fairest reading acknowledges both the harm done by later uses of the scene and the text's own insistence that the warning is addressed to insiders, and that the insiders who most need it now are Christians.

observe: What three things does the devil ask Jesus to do, and which passage of Deuteronomy does Jesus answer with each time?
What words from Isaiah does Jesus read in Nazareth, and at what point does he stop reading?
List the things Jesus does in Capernaum on the Sabbath and in the evening (verses 31-41). What word does Luke use for how Jesus deals with the demon and the fever?
interpret: Why does each temptation begin with the Son of God title, and how do Jesus' answers show what kind of Son he is?
Why might Jesus stop before ‘the day of vengeance’, and what does ‘today this Scripture is fulfilled’ claim about him?
Why did the examples of the widow of Zarephath and Naaman make the people of Nazareth so angry?
apply: The devil quoted Scripture to tempt Jesus. How can you tell when the Bible is being used to serve someone's own ends, including your own?
Who are the poor, the captives, and the oppressed in your community, and what would good news mean to them?
Where might familiarity with Jesus, or a sense that God owes you, keep you from receiving what he is doing?
